effect_mechanism: On tropical peat, rewetting removes the drainage stress that keeps the site degraded, and where seed can still arrive the native community returns without planting: native peat-swamp-forest tree species were found growing spontaneously, at high density, in the most rewetted conditions of a restoration area (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to deliver enhanced biodiversity alongside litter supply to the upper peat, a stabilised microclimate and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
conditionality: Neither unit isolates the practice, so this row carries direction and nothing about size or speed. The Sumatran observation is explicitly a best case: every plot lay close to remaining forest, so seed arrival is easy, and the regrowth cannot be separated from the earlier clearing or from that seed proximity - no share of the outcome is attributed to rewetting alone (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). The companion statement is a potential the authors expect, not a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both come from upper-middle-income Southeast Asian peatlands, neither reports a comparison with an intact reference nor a time to recovery, and neither is from a low-income or farmed landscape - so for a humid-tropics scan this is a plausible-direction flag that needs local monitoring evidence before any magnitude is claimed, with distance to remaining forest the first thing to check on the ground.

effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping landscapes the benefit comes from adding aquatic habitat where almost none remains. Catchment-scale wetland creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness, with the accumulation curve still rising after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity in a landscape whose small waters had increased by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Establishment choices last: the planted basin remained more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than its unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7].
conditionality: Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Sweden and Ohio, and neither is a restoration of a lost wetland: they are wetlands created under a programme designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5] and a pair of pumped experimental basins [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The 30% figure is a design condition on habitat density, not a measured effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is a regional accumulation across many wetlands, so it does not promise a gain at a single created site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio comparison is planting against natural colonisation within created wetlands rather than wetland against no wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Nothing here was measured in a tropical or low-income rainfed system, and no unit reports how the gain changes as the wetland ages.

effect_mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost, and the new basins can reach the standard of the old ones. Dual-purpose created wetlands sustained alpha, beta and gamma diversity similar to that of natural lentic water bodies in the region [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2], and the pollution-sensitive stoneflies, mayflies and caddisflies made up almost twice as large a share of richness in the created wetlands, 19%, as in the reference ponds, 10% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. Catchment-scale creation benefited landscape biodiversity, particularly where aquatic habitat density rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness with no asymptote after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity where small waters had risen by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Planting at creation left a lasting mark: the planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years on than the unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. In the Amu Darya delta of Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are reported to present adequate living conditions for fauna and flora and an adequate substitute for the drained part of Lake Ayaskala [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2].
conditionality: Most of these findings state a direction without an effect size. Two of the strongest results are comparisons against mature natural ponds rather than against a no-wetland baseline, so they say the created wetlands are as good as the existing ones, not how much the landscape gained by building them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. The measured evidence is temperate and high-income, Sweden and Ohio, and the Swedish wetlands were designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is regional and cumulative, not a promise for a single basin [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio contrast is planting against natural colonisation inside created wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The one lower-income unit, from Uzbekistan, is an evaluator's statement resting on anecdotal site visits and committee reports, about wetlands that arose within a bundled drainage and irrigation programme rather than being built for habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]; no tropical or lower-income measurement is present, and no unit reports whether the invertebrate advantage holds as the wetlands age and fill with sediment.

effect_mechanism: Raising the water table and removing the degrading pressure is what allows peatland vegetation to re-establish, and adding an active revegetation step is what makes it quick. Enhanced restoration using moss-layer transfer brought Sphagnum cover towards, and potentially past, intact levels and reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7); basic rewetting and tree felling produced marked recovery on a multi-decadal path (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2); and the systematic review's own summary is that active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10). In Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline (ev_wgy_blr_7). Where only the upper peat layer had been removed, biological structure recovered immediately (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10). On tropical peat the same lever appears as native peat-swamp-forest trees regrowing spontaneously in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
conditionality: Structure returning is not function returning, and neither is the same as matching an intact site. In restored peatlands, Sphagnum cover and peatland specialist cover remained well below intact peatlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1), and where biological structure did recover immediately the biogeochemical functioning of the same peatlands stayed statistically below reference decades later (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10) - so a row that reads as a biodiversity gain against a degraded baseline still carries a shortfall against the intact reference, and the comparisons must not be netted against each other. The restoration method decides whether there is any result at all within an investment horizon: passive restoration was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5), with specialist cover stagnating or further deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to cause a decline in specialist diversity, a response the authors could not predict reliably (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8). The Belarus result shows the same dependence on active work: it fell short of the target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent from the donor bogs for three years so only 70 ha were planted or sown, and reed and cattail were first to appear on the rest, expected to give way to sedge as the sites develop (ev_wgy_blr_7). The temperate and boreal evidence is substantial and mostly high-income; the tropical units are thin, bundled with clearing and seed proximity, and partly a stated potential rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4), so transferring this row to a tropical peat landscape rests on mechanism, not on matched evidence. A review of agricultural use of wetlands adds the other side of the ledger, what draining the existing peatland cost in the first place: agriculture in the Dutch wetlands, particularly in the past century, has been shown to be non-sustainable through subsidence and devastating for wetland biodiversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_3), and agriculture on South-East Asian tropical peat soils has resulted in irreversible biodiversity losses (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_4). The review ties both losses to intensive drained use (fertiliser, pesticides and deeper drainage for crops such as oil palm) rather than to drainage alone. These units describe the degraded state that rewetting starts from, not anything rewetting achieved, so they are carried as context and enter through the existing-wetland home-family route rather than as measured restoration outcomes; the word irreversible is a further warning that the gain above is a partial recovery, not a return of what was lost.

justification.mechanism: Raising the water table and removing the degrading pressure is what allows peatland vegetation to re-establish, and adding an active revegetation step is what makes it quick. Enhanced restoration using moss-layer transfer brought Sphagnum cover towards, and potentially past, intact levels and reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7); basic rewetting and tree felling produced marked recovery on a multi-decadal path (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2); and the systematic review's own summary is that active restoration or replacement measures are needed to speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10). In Belarus, vegetation mapping after rewetting 950 ha of the Dokudovskoe cut-over peatland found Phragmites-sedge communities on at least 398 ha, against no more than 20 ha at baseline (ev_wgy_blr_7). Where only the upper peat layer had been removed, biological structure recovered immediately (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10). On tropical peat the same lever appears as native peat-swamp-forest trees regrowing spontaneously in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
justification.conditionality: Structure returning is not function returning, and neither is the same as matching an intact site. In restored peatlands, Sphagnum cover and peatland specialist cover remained well below intact peatlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1), and where biological structure did recover immediately the biogeochemical functioning of the same peatlands stayed statistically below reference decades later (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_10) - so a row that reads as a biodiversity gain against a degraded baseline still carries a shortfall against the intact reference, and the comparisons must not be netted against each other. The restoration method decides whether there is any result at all within an investment horizon: passive restoration was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5), with specialist cover stagnating or further deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to cause a decline in specialist diversity, a response the authors could not predict reliably (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8). The Belarus result shows the same dependence on active work: it fell short of the target of at least 700 ha, sedge seed was practically absent from the donor bogs for three years so only 70 ha were planted or sown, and reed and cattail were first to appear on the rest, expected to give way to sedge as the sites develop (ev_wgy_blr_7). The temperate and boreal evidence is substantial and mostly high-income; the tropical units are thin, bundled with clearing and seed proximity, and partly a stated potential rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4), so transferring this row to a tropical peat landscape rests on mechanism, not on matched evidence. A review of agricultural use of wetlands adds the other side of the ledger, what draining the existing peatland cost in the first place: agriculture in the Dutch wetlands, particularly in the past century, has been shown to be non-sustainable through subsidence and devastating for wetland biodiversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_3), and agriculture on South-East Asian tropical peat soils has resulted in irreversible biodiversity losses (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_4). The review ties both losses to intensive drained use (fertiliser, pesticides and deeper drainage for crops such as oil palm) rather than to drainage alone. These units describe the degraded state that rewetting starts from, not anything rewetting achieved, so they are carried as context and enter through the existing-wetland home-family route rather than as measured restoration outcomes; the word irreversible is a further warning that the gain above is a partial recovery, not a return of what was lost.

effect_mechanism: In the humid tropics every unit in this pool is one side of the greenhouse-gas ledger, and no source weighs the sides against each other. On the carbon dioxide side, rewetting drained tropical peat slows subsidence and the peat decomposition it indicates [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1], with a stated ceiling on what in-plantation water management can buy back [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1] and a drained-forest case where raising the water level hardly reduced the surface flux because root respiration dominates [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]. On the methane side, the paired Kalimantan sites show fluxes moving in opposite directions after damming, with the authors reading the overall effect on the annual methane budget as small [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]. Vegetation regrowth on open restored peat is reported as still too small to compensate for carbon losses from decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3].
conditionality: No class is stated because no unit here reports a net carbon dioxide equivalent balance: the subsidence-based accounting integrates the gases without separating them, the flux studies report one gas at a time, and the question that decides the class — whether methane gains exceed the carbon dioxide saved — is unanswered for tropical sites. One source states the gap outright for the field as a whole. A single measured net balance from a rewetted tropical site would let this cell state a class; until then the carbon dioxide savings and the methane movements sit side by side [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6].

effect_mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. effect_mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. effect_mechanism: Wetlands feed the households beside them directly, through crops grown in them and fish caught from them. In Uganda's Kyoga plains households report to derive about half of the household food from the wetlands, particularly through cultivation of paddy rice [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_2], and over 75% of respondents acknowledged that wetlands directly contribute to their household food security [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_4]. In Laos, protecting fishery conservation zones safeguarded and increased local fish variety and density; the fish wash into farmers' fields and ponds in the flood season, farmers may catch them, and farmers said this provides them with more food [ev_wgy_lao_4].
conditionality: The food gains describe what households already draw from existing wetlands, or from protected fishery zones inside existing wetlands, as reported by the households themselves; none is a change measured after rewetting or restoring a degraded wetland [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_2, ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_4, ev_wgy_lao_4]. The same Uganda survey points the other way on one measure: keeping other variables equal, the likelihood of experiencing food insecurity increases by 23% if a household participates in collection of wetland products for food security [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_1]. That is an association across households, not an effect of the wetland, but it warns that the households leaning on wetland food are not the food-secure ones. The only matched evaluation of an actual restoration project, the Green Climate Fund endline in Uganda, detected no statistically significant difference between treatment and comparison households [ev_food_security_fp034e_4], and that project restricted access inside demarcated wetlands. For design, the evidence suggests food benefits follow where restoration keeps or opens household use of wetland crops and fish, and are at risk where it closes access.

effect_mechanism: The evidence speaks to a short and a long horizon. In the short term, rewetting ends drainage-based cropping: food crops such as potatoes and carrots become unsuitable [ev_wgy_qa_6], high and low water-table uses cannot share a peatland [ev_wgy_ram_17], and paludicrops are mostly non-edible [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]; Finland reports a minor national but a local effect [ev_wgy_qa_5]. In the long term, keeping peat drained also loses production: subsidence on deep SE Asian peat may cause loss of agricultural production once gravity drainage fails [ev_agricultural_production_value_hooi12_3], and the drained Mega Rice Project land proved largely unsuitable for rice, threatening local livelihoods [ev_agricultural_production_value_ritz13_9].
conditionality: The class and its evidence disagree in kind. The positive direction comes from studies of draining tropical peat (oil palm, Acacia, the Mega Rice Project), which document the cost of keeping peat drained, not a measured yield after rewetting; it is an avoided-future-loss argument. The measured-style evidence on rewetting itself, all European, points to a near-term production loss. No low-income source. Treat as: rewetting costs production now and may avoid larger losses later on deep, subsiding tropical peat.

effect_mechanism: All the units here concern wet use of tropical peat and come from reviews citing other work. On the gain side, sago, a crop that grows on shallow peat without drainage, is cited at an internal rate of return of 12.9–19%, rising to 17.4–19.2% once environmental benefits are counted [ev_economic_return_tan21_9], and the same review concludes from NPV, IRR and BCR that paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit, while adding in the same sentence that its benefits relative to conventional drainage-based crops are still too low and that not all costs and externalities are documented [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]. On the loss side, communities that have relied on oil palm cultivation will find it challenging to participate in peatland restoration, since rewetting may entail lower productivity and financial return for their crops [ev_household_income_mish21_5].
conditionality: The direction is a slight gain carried by modelled returns to a wet crop, and the loss for oil-palm households is kept as harm to those adopters, not averaged away. What separates them is the starting point: a household that can grow and sell sago or another wet crop gains a modest return, while a household giving up drained oil palm loses income relative to what it had. effect_mechanism: The matched evidence in low-income settings shows no household gain. The Uganda GCF evaluation found that awareness, crop diversification and adaptation changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income or asset accumulation; total income was lower among treated households, significant at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income was close to zero difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3]. In Kabale, Uganda, the national wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1], and 22% of respondents earned no income at all from the wetlands, leaving them no incentive to conserve, a statement about existing use rather than a change from restoration [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_3]. The only gain is reported in Uzbekistan, where the revival of fish, muskrat skin and reed production from wetlands formed by the project contributed to a substantial increase in income for residents [ev_household_income_uzicr_1].
conditionality: The sides are a matched evaluation and a completion-report assertion, and they differ in what the wetland gave households. The loss is in Uganda, where rehabilitation came with restrictions on cultivation inside demarcated wetlands alongside livelihood packages, and treated households had lower total income at endline, significant only at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income showed close to zero difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3]. The gain is in Uzbekistan, where new wetlands formed along drainage collectors revived harvestable fish, muskrat skin and reeds; the completion report asserts the income increase rather than measuring it [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]. The separator is whether the wetland opens a product households can sell or closes land they farmed. Most of the weight is neither: the Uganda evaluation found no measurable improvement in income or asset accumulation, and the Kabale policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1]. Treat restoration in low-income settings as income-neutral to negative unless the design adds an adequate, well-targeted livelihood payment or product channel.

effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, household income has been found both to fall and to rise with wetland restoration. Losses follow land taken out of farming and the size of compensation: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw per capita income fall by 0.338 log points, with the authors reporting a significant negative impact [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6] while total, farm and non-agricultural income fell without reaching significance [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_5], and 56.9% of surveyed households said income decreased after joining the compensation policy, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]; in SE Asia, communities relying on oil palm face lower productivity and financial return under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5]. Gains come through other channels: the same Poyang households gained transfer income (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4]; Working for Wetlands in South Africa employed people previously without stable income [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2]; tropical paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]; and in Belarus indirect benefits reached agro-ecotourism businesses and wild-berry marketing [ev_wgy_blr_2]. Newer project accounts add to the gain side: in Viet Nam's U Minh Thuong buffer zone, Green Contracts for alternative fire-free income sources resulted in a doubling of annual incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1]; in Riau, 75% of the 152 respondents registered monthly income increase of more than USD 35 from selling community-garden harvest [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2]; and in South Sumatra fishponds inside a rewetted canal system generated 18,700,000 IDR from the 2019 harvest, which the authors call not yet optimal [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. Paludiculture crops now count for the peatland family, and they add to the gain side, all modelled or second-hand: sago's internal rate of return is cited at 12.9–19%, rising to 17.4–19.2% when environmental benefits are counted [ev_economic_return_tan21_9]; in Central Kalimantan, dragon fruit, candlenut and mangosteen were modelled at NPVs of more than €40,000/ha, comparable to oil palm [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1]; mature sago stands in Riau are cited at revenues of up to 1500 euro per ha per year [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]; and water spinach in a South Sumatran agro-sylvofishery project had a benefit-cost ratio of 2.97 by the project manager's account [ev_wet_econret_budi20_1].
conditionality: What separates the sides is the channel: households lose where farmland or drained-peat crops are given up and compensation is small or absent, and gain through transfers, wages on restoration works, or local businesses [ev_wgy_poy_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wgy_blr_2]. Time also matters: the Poyang loss was no longer significant by the later panel round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. Product is a further separator: crops that grow on wet or shallow-drained peat and find a market carry the modelled gains [ev_economic_return_tan21_9, ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]. Compensation size, who receives it, and whether a saleable wet crop is built in are the levers a project controls. The crop gains are weaker than they look: the Kalimantan model excludes the cost of restoring drained peat, such as canal dams, and its most profitable crop, dragon fruit, still needs some drainage [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1]; the sago revenue is for mature stands that take years to reach first harvest [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]; the sago returns are cited from other studies [ev_economic_return_tan21_9]; and the water-spinach ratio is a project figure for a community demonstration, not a household income [ev_wet_econret_budi20_1]. A Central Kalimantan report of income losses in villages that had stopped fire use was rejected at review by Pete Steward, who was not confident it could be included, and is no longer counted; the row stays split without it. The Vietnamese and Riau gains come from alternative livelihoods bundled with the restoration rather than from the restored peat, are self-reported and have no comparison group [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1, ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2], and the Sumatran fish income is a community demonstration-project total, not a household figure [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. effect_mechanism: Restoring floodplains and lakebeds mostly lowers household income, because it retires farmland or restricts access, and payments or wages make up for it only in part. Where farmland is retired income falls: at Poyang Lake per capita income fell by 0.338 log points [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2], and 56.9% of households in a compensation survey said income decreased, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]; the Uganda Green Climate Fund matched evaluation found no measurable welfare gain and lower total income at the 10 per cent level [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2]. Smaller gains come through transfers and wages: the same Poyang households gained transfer income (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4], and Working for Wetlands in South Africa employed people previously without stable income [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2]. Separately, households already draw substantial income from existing wetlands: cultivating the reclaimed Cyabayaga wetland in Rwanda contributed $ 1901 U.S. per household per year, 74% of gross margin, against $ 84 U.S. (24%) in Rugeramigozi [ev_wet_hhinc_naba12_1, ev_wet_hhinc_naba12_2], and selling wetland products earned an average Ugandan household UGX 99,208 (approx. USD 36) a month [ev_wet_hhinc_tury13_3]; in Laos, farmers reported more fish catches near protected zones [ev_wgy_lao_5].
conditionality: What separates the sides is whether restoration takes land or access away from households and whether payments or wages replace it [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3]. Where restoration would rewet farmed wetland like Cyabayaga, the household cost could be large; where it protects wetland that households keep using, as in Laos, losses are smaller [ev_wet_hhinc_naba12_1, ev_wgy_lao_5]. Compensation sized to forgone income and paid to the actual users is the design condition. Several positive units do not measure a benefit of restoration: the Rwanda and Uganda income figures are what households stand to lose if access is restricted, the Vermont avoided-flood-damage ratio is a society-level benefit [ev_economic_return_gour20_2], and the Poyang transfer gain is a component of income whose total fell. The measured restoration studies, Poyang and the Uganda evaluation, are on the negative or null side; the Poyang loss was no longer significant by the later panel round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7].

On the only quantity measured here - the share of storm rainfall leaving as storm discharge - restoration changed nothing at either restored site relative to the bare, unrestored control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).

The unit behind this row is a runoff-coefficient null (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), and the paper's own conclusion is that restoration altered the timing and peak of storm delivery while leaving the volume of runoff produced unchanged. effect_mechanism: A created wetland works as a reactor placed in the flow path: residence time rises, nitrogen is removed by plant uptake and denitrification and phosphorus settles with sediment, so a share of the incoming load leaves the water. Across created and restored freshwater wetlands that is a measured net removal of total nitrogen and total phosphorus, both as mass rates and as a share of the incoming load (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_1, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_2, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_5), and nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted into the tenth year of a created riverine pair (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3). Where new wetlands are put matters more than how many: modelled placement in the highest nitrogen-surplus areas removes far more nitrogen than placement on non-agricultural land, at a higher cost because it takes cropland out of production (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3), and the gain flattens as restoration spreads beyond the hotspots (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5). Created wetlands can be designed to hold nutrients and carry species diversity at the same time rather than trading them off (ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6).
conditionality: Creating a wetland on nutrient-enriched farmland can reverse the sign. Negative phosphorus removal - the wetland exporting phosphorus rather than retaining it - was reported in a minority of the reviewed wetlands, and most of those had been created on former cropland or cattle pasture, where soil rich in phosphorus from its cropping history can release after construction (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_6); the rest were new wetlands released from initially phosphorus-rich sediments. That is the setting a rural scan targets, so legacy soil phosphorus belongs in the design brief. At site level a created basin exported total phosphorus in its tenth year while its twin barely retained any, after years of consistent retention (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3), and sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment and phosphorus services age out while the nitrogen service holds. A substantial minority of individual wetlands showed no demonstrable nitrogen removal (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_8), and net annual release of nitrogen, though rare, has been observed (ev_nutrient_removal_land16_9). The quantified ceiling claims are modelled, not measured, and every unit is high-income temperate - inflows in the review included treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff, so the pooled efficiency is not a farmland-only number.

effect_mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, generalises this: disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7).
conditionality: The gain is measured against the degraded starting point, and against that baseline restored extraction sites leak less (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). Measured against their intact natural counterparts the same restored sites leaked more nutrients and carbon, associated with greater water-table variation (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_4); that is incomplete recovery towards an intact peatland, not harm, and the two comparisons must not be netted. The real reversals are in the Ramsar report's cited synthesis. In some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term (ev_wgy_ram_8); and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens, rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, internal eutrophication (ev_wgy_ram_9). Agricultural peat is exactly the land a rural scan would target, so a downstream nutrient pulse in the early years, and a sustained phosphorus problem on fertilised fens, should be planned for rather than assumed away. The measured case in this pool found no significant water-quality improvement and no significant reduction in aqueous carbon losses after rewetting an eroding upland blanket peat, with dissolved organic carbon rising non-significantly afterwards (ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null); the quantity measured there is dissolved organic carbon routed to the nearest water-quality outcome, not nutrients, and water colour did change. Everything here is boreal or temperate peat in high-income countries or unspecified settings; nothing covers tropical peat or a farmed low- or lower-middle-income catchment, and the Ramsar statements give direction without magnitude or site.

effect_mechanism: The direction in this scope rests on the general hydrological function rather than on a measured restoration: wetlands store water from precipitation and slowly release it to the surrounding environment, which can recharge groundwater aquifers and maintain atmospheric water cycles [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. Restoring or protecting a wetland is expected to restore that storage and slow release, and so to ease a water deficit downstream of it.
conditionality: This cell is thin, and its units pull in different directions. The positive unit is a functional statement about wetlands in general, offered as a key message rather than as the measured result of any restoration, with no magnitude, no time to effect and no country attached [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. The other is a timescale caveat from a narrative review: numerous studies of peatland rewetting suggest that many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the initial few years after restoration, because of earlier changes in peat structure and consolidation caused by degradation [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. That caveat cuts both ways — short monitoring windows may hide a benefit as easily as they may flatter an early result — but it means nothing here establishes what a restored wetland delivers, to whom, or when. Nothing in this scope measures a farm-level water supply, and neither unit names the income context it was observed in; treat the direction as an expectation to be tested in the pilot rather than as evidence of a delivered gain.
